comment: Ground truth for the user's own library (established by ear + analysis). Values are DETECTOR-relative: rot = allowed values of (downbeat index % beatsPerBar) on the detector's own beat grid; bpb = expected beatsPerBar. null = no stable ground truth, report only. reject:true = the detector must return null (no steady pulse deserves a metronome). barLenAt = [{t, n}]: the bar covering time t must be n beats long — the only anchor that catches an un-modelled meter change (a uniform-4 grid reports 4 everywhere and silently stretches the odd bar). Sourced from the published score AND verified against the audio before being committed.

Pink Floyd - Wish You Were Here.note: Anchor minted from harmonic evidence, EAR-CHECK PENDING. Unlike Sixteen Tons (where the harmonic arbiter decided a song built to defeat it), this song is the arbiter's ideal case and the score says so explicitly: ONE chord per bar, every change on a downbeat, no exceptions. 195.988s carries a 7-beat chord change to C, sits on a bar line of the majority parity, and the "How I wish, how I wish you were here" line starts 0.55s later (vocal pickup after the downbeat) — score bar 46, the top of Verse 2. Three agreeing signals.
Pink Floyd - Wish You Were Here.scoreNote: OUR OCTAVE IS DOUBLED, AND FOR ONCE THAT IS NOT TASTE — it is measured against a published fact. Official Pink Floyd tab (verified artist: the type=900 search returns FIVE artists for this title and the Avril Lavigne trap is live): quarter = 60 printed once at bar 1, UNIFORM 4/4 across all 83 bars, NO meter change, NO rall./ritard./a tempo/fermata anywhere including the fade, and ONE CHORD PER BAR throughout — a change every 4.000 s, always on a downbeat. The score certifies its own uniformity three independent ways: 83 bars x 4/4 at 60 = 332.000 s exactly, matching its stated duration; its syllable clock gives 4.000 s per bar across every span including 14 bars through the solo; and multi-bar rests (which cannot span a meter change) tile the whole song across four tracks. MEASURED against our grid 2026-08-03: we ship 122.95 bpm with 172 bars of 1.952 s. The chord decode over guitar+piano+other with a bass root bonus gives a MEDIAN CHORD RUN OF 8 OF OUR BEATS = 3.90 s = 0.98 SCORE BARS — the score's one-chord-per-bar rhythm is present in the recording, and our bar is exactly half of it. The clincher is parity: of the 54 chord changes landing on one of our bar lines, 47 are on odd-numbered bars and 7 on even. A correct octave splits evenly; a doubled grid puts them all on one parity, which is what we see. So the true downbeats are our ODD bars and a halving that keeps that parity reproduces the score. Recording runs ~2.5% slower than notated (3.90 vs 4.000 s per bar) — a real performance, not a tempo change. THIS IS A NEGATIVE CONTROL for the meter repair operator: uniform 4/4 certified three ways, so the operator must insert NOTHING here. Two caveats: our copy is the album master WITH the radio-tuning intro (lyrics.json opens on four spoken lines, "And disciplinary remains mercifully" etc.) while the score has no such intro and starts the guitar at bar 2, so the score clock has no shared origin with our audio — anchor by lyric, never by score bar number; and the score's own syllable clock carries a 1.000 s lead-in offset against its 332.000 s duration figure, so even internally its absolute times are not the recording's.

Our own file names no artist at all (id3 title "Sixteen Tons (Am, +2)", a backing track labelled by key, 2:36, 123.2 bpm), so the recording is UNIDENTIFIED and the notated quarter = 140 is not comparable to it. Treat the METER as portable ground truth and the TEMPO map as arrangement-only. Meter: UNIFORM 4/4, 84 bars, sections all exact multiples of 4 (Intro 1-4, V 5-12, Ch 13-20, Pre 21-24, ...), no repeats. Ford-only: one ritard bar 79 at quarter = 40 (6.000 s vs 1.714 s). WHY THIS SONG IS A PHASE TRAP, and why the check mattered: the score prints TWO chords per bar with the chord ATTACK ON THE OFFBEATS, boom-chick guitar (bass root on 1 and 3, full strum on 2 and 4), FINGER SNAP ON 2 AND 4 the whole song, and walking-bass eighths on alternate bars — the loudest harmonic AND transient events both sit on the backbeat, so an onset- or chord-driven vote has everything it needs to land a beat off. This anchor's barAt was re-minted in July when the harmonic arbiter overruled the original ear GT (+0.54 chord-mass gain), i.e. decided by exactly the cue this song defeats. MEASURED 2026-08-03, phase-folded on the COMMITTED ANCHOR itself (not on project.json, which is a stale detVersion 12 grid): snap-band (1.5-8 kHz) flux is 21.1 / 36.4 / 9.4 / 33.1 % across beats 1-4, i.e. backbeat 69.5% vs 30.5% — the snap peaks on OUR 2 and 4, exactly where the score puts it. Also: verse openings are guitar/brass/piano TACET (voice + offbeat snap only; bass rests the whole first bar of 5/25/45/65) so they carry no harmonic information at all; and the file is flagged swung/shuffled eighths (is_triplet) while its exported syllable times are STRAIGHT eighths — the swing is a feel flag, not baked into the data.

A future bar decoder must reason about meter AT THE NOTATED LEVEL.
